title: Doings That Happened Twenty Years Ago (reprinting June 1883)
text: Arthur Marshall was looking for his pants Monday. He lost them in Sunday's flood. ... In the absence of trains our livery men are enjoying a harvest. ... On Thursday night of last week three bridges on the south branch of the Weeping Water were carried out by the raise in that stream, and lodged against the railroad bridge near Avoca. ... probably more water fell in this vicinity than ever before. It poured through the streets in torrents, carrying boxes, empty barrels and every thing loose in its course, cellars were flooded ... At five o'clock Sunday morning the inhabitants of the town were aroused to the imminent peril of that portion of the village located on low ground on both sides of the creek. The water soon rose until the iron bridge on Randolph street was three feet under water. The homes of Mrs. Gray and Mrs. Sewell Reed located on the bottoms were flooded ... something like $50.00 was raised by subscription and given these ladies to in part reimburse them for their loss. The Randolph St. bridge was held in place by chains fastened to trees on the banks. Sunday forenoon Henry Hogget was endeavoring to ride through the intervening water to the Randolph bridge, when his horse was ridden off the high grade. Henry was dismounted and as he could not swim his life was in peril, but fortunately he caught hold of a small tree and held on until he was rescued by men in a boat but only in the nick of time for in a moment afterwards the oil house of P. S. Barnes came floating down and struck the tree to which he had been clinging and buried it beneath the angry waters. P. S. Barnes lost his warehouse and a portion of its contents valued at $250. ... Wat Gordon, four miles west, lost $100 worth of hogs, all his bees and a milk cow. ... Deacon Beach had two fat hogs and several rods of fence washed away.

title: Aerial photo after the flood
text: Above is aerial photo of Weeping Water taken Tuesday morning after water had receded. The circle indicates the location of the east bridge prior to the flood. The two (X's) mark the locations of the Chub Rector and Lee Straton homes. Both homes were completely demolished and very few of their furnishings were recovered. —Photo courtesy of Nell Munkres

title: What is left of the east bridge
text: Close-up shot of what is left of the east bridge leading to the business section of Weeping Water. Photo was taken about ... last Tuesday morning after the creek had receded about as [fast as it] rose Monday night. Water level was the highest in the history of this community. —Staff Photo

title: No Funds Now Available For Bridge Repair
text: Gov. Val Peterson Saturday afternoon declared Cass County and several other southeastern Nebraska counties as emergency areas following last week's flood and asked for an appropriation of between $350,000 and $500,000 for emergency bridge repair. The watersheds included in the governor's statement are the Weeping Water creek, Little Nemaha, Nemaha and upper Big Blue. Gen. Lewis A. Pick, chief of army engineers and Brig. Gen. Samuel Sturgis, Missouri river division engineer, also spoke at the meeting held at Lincoln municipal airport ... According to reports received at the conference, Cass county suffered $152,400 damage with 310 bridges damaged, of which ten actually went out. ... Gen. Pick expressed surprise when he was informed that several of the bridges damaged in the flood of 1947 had not been replaced or repaired. He said that if plans suggested two years ago in the Missouri Valley development had been adopted, at least two-thirds of the damage from last week's flood could have been eliminated.

title: Norris Hatchery: FLOOD SPECIAL chicks
text: We surely appreciate the wonderful response we have had the past week on our FLOOD SPECIAL chicks. You really helped us out. We will keep the same special prices in effect for the rest of the season. Better hurry and get [some] of those flood chicks. Only a few more hatching. NORRIS HATCHERY

title: Community Club to take action
text: It was pointed out at the meeting that because of the bridge washouts in Weeping Water and its trade territory, farmers are forced to drive several extra miles to reach town to do their shopping. It was decided to try and send a delegation of business and professional men, farmers and all other interested parties to meet with the Cass county commissioners yesterday, to see what plans have been made to repair and replace the bridges lost in last week's flood.

title: High water swamps town after 7 inch rain
text: The 7.42 inches of rain which fell in Weeping Water on Tuesday evening, June 12, added to the already swollen Weeping Water Creek. The creek went out of its banks for the second time in three years. The most severe damage included the homes of Bruce Sorensen and Larry Houseman. The Sorensens do not intend to move back into their house which was flooded for the third consecutive year. The tennis courts were ruined as was the equipment building on the school practice field. Fire Chief Ted Wilson called it a "real disaster." He estimated it would take two to three weeks to clean up. Firemen and Rescue Squad personnel plus many other volunteers never went to bed Tuesday evening. Because of a malfunctioning siren, emergency vehicles were used to drive through the city warning people of the flood threat and tornado warnings. Approximately 25 people were evacuated from their homes and sought shelter somewhere else. From approximately 4:30 a.m. to 6 a.m. on Wednesday, the flood water was over both bridges in the city. The Avoca and Manley volunteer fire departments assisted in evacuating people.

title: High water damage inspected
text: HIGH WATER DAMAGE—Inspected east of Weeping Water by, from left, ASCS Manager Dan Steinkruger, Commissioner Hilton Rogers and Congressman Doug Bereuter.

title: Walkway washed away
text: WALKWAY WASHED AWAY—The pedestrian approach to the west bridge over Weeping Water Creek is no more. Marty Rupp inspects the damage. (Fred Ward Photo).

title: High water (continued)
text: Lightning apparently was the cause of a fire in a hay barn at the Willis Lorensen farm east of Weeping Water on Tuesday evening. Water had washed out a bridge north of his place so the fire department had to circle around and enter from the south. The hay barn was a total loss. While moving furniture to higher ground, Larry Sorensen cut his hand and it required seven stitches to sew it up. Many, many homes had basements flooded from the heavy rains and high water. The Tom Beins home had six feet of water in the basement. ... The water also backed up into the Fire House. The Mark Hohmann home was sandbagged although that didn't keep the water from entering the garage. The basement walls at the Bill Neumeister home caved in as they did at the Larry Houseman home. The pits at the rock quarries are full of water. ... Mr. and Mrs. Chester Hopper provided breakfast for volunteers on Wednesday morning at the D & B Diner.

title: Bruce Sorensen residence
text: BRUCE SORENSEN RESIDENCE—Absorbed high water damage. (Fred Ward Photo).

title: No travel here
text: NO TRAVEL HERE—The footbridge to Swede Town. (Fred Ward Photo).

title: Good fishing
text: GOOD FISHING—Mitch Miller of Weeping Water displays his catch at the railroad tracks. (Fred Ward Photo).

title: Around Town: the month of storms
text: So June is the month of roses and perfect days — not so, this year. June is the month of storms as in evidence Tuesday night, June 12, when 7.5 inches of rain fell in a short time causing floods, so all around town it is mud, flooded basements and an aftermath mess. Just two years ago, June, 1982, the Republican headlines read "Rampaging creek sweeps away city bridge, inundates several homes in Weeping Water" — the 80-ft long single lane bridge spanning the Weeping Water creek buckled and slipped into the water and was carried 40 yards downstream.

title: Sign of the times
text: SIGN OF THE TIMES—Floodwaters from the Weeping Water Creek toppled the sign at the U.S. 34 bridge west of Union.

title: County soil erosion damage estimated at $10 million
text: Last Tuesday's storm left Cass County residents with a monumental clean up job and a very large tab. ... It was significantly more intense than the June 15th storm of 1982, says the Lower Platte South Natural Resources District (NRD), and nearly was as intense as the devastating storm of May, 1950. For example, peak flows measured by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) at their monitoring station near Union were about the same last Tuesday as they were in 1950. ... Unofficial rainfall amounts were measured at 7.42 inches in a nine-hour period at Weeping Water, 5.50 inches at Murdock, 5.40 inches at Elmwood, and 4.30 inches at Union. ... According to Bill Best, of the U.S. Soil Conservation Service (SCS), 225,000 acres of cropland was damaged by erosion. About 30 percent of the corn crop was lost ... Erosion damage was estimated at $10 million ... The NRD general manager said, "A flood control project such as the one presently being proposed on Weeping Water Creek would certainly have reduced the damages from this flood. It would not eliminate the flooding, but the proposed project would have controlled a lot of it."

title: Bridge at Randolph Street gone
text: Weeping Water residents look across the Weeping Water creek from both sides of Randolph St., where the bridge was washed away shortly after 4 a.m. Tuesday, June 15.

title: Rampaging Creek Sweeps Away City Bridge, Inundates Several Homes In Weeping Water
text: Rampaging Creek Sweeps Away City Bridge, Inundates Several Homes In Weeping Water

title: Volunteers wade toward Eldora Ave.
text: Above, a group of volunteers make their way through the floodwaters toward dry pavement on Eldora Ave. in Weeping Water. The group was returning from a check of houses in danger of being taken by water.

title: The Sorensen home
text: The home of Tom and Betty Sorensen, which is situated along the north bank of the Weeping Water creek, was flooded, forcing the occupants to flee.

title: Volunteers worked through the night
text: Volunteers worked throughout the night into the sun-up hours evacuating residents and their household goods and monitoring the flood. Above, Tom Hasenyager, Weeping Water chief of police, listens as an unidentified woman volunteer gives him some information.

title: Rampaging creek (story)
text: Residents of Riverside addition in southeast Weeping Water, known locally as "Swedetown," were alerted and several left their homes until the flood waters started abating later in the morning. ... Several pieces of heavy equipment in the Martin Marietta quarries just west of Weeping Water were covered by the flooding creek. The receding flood waters did create a veritable paradise for fishermen, who had a field day hand-catching many carp and a scattering of catfish which were trapped between the rails of the Missouri Pacific railroad tracks which run through town, just north of the creek. Bridge Goes: The 80-foot-long single lane bridge spanning the Weeping Water creek at Randolph St. was a flood casualty. The bridge buckled and slipped into the water in the pre-dawn hours Tuesday. It was carried 140 yards downstream where it came to rest against some trees. ... Maj. Gen. Edward Binder of the Nebraska national guard flew into the Weeping Water airport, arriving at approximately 7:30 a.m. Tuesday to speak with town officials and to view the damage.

title: Flood Water Causes Extensive Damage Locally
text: Excessive rains along the Weeping Water Watershed late Friday turned the usually placid Weeping Water Creek into a rushing stream, as water surged over its banks, flooding fields and other lowlands along its way. ... By 7 p.m. Friday, 14 or so feet of water was pouring into the underground operation [at the Kerford Quarries]. ... The city park, its tennis courts and play area west of the old bridge were flooded. Youngsters were attempting to catch fish trapped on the tennis court Saturday. Flood waters reached within 12 feet of the Missouri Pacific railroad tracks. ... the Thomas Sorensen home once more threatened. Waters came almost to their doorstep, lacking a few feet of invading the main floor. The family was up all night watching. ... Residents having gardens in the lowlands between the town's two bridges were out Friday night, hastily pulling up any garden produce that could be salvaged. During one phase of the flood, North Commercial St. was literally part of the creek. ... East of Weeping Water on the Vernon Duwe farm, cattle were reportedly neck deep in water Friday evening ... Larry Hanson, driving out to help rescue the cattle, found his vehicle going under the flood water upon returning to the vehicle. Maurice Hammons managed to move his endangered livestock to safety east of town and Mr. and Mrs. Emery Hansen moved their pigs twice.

title: From the west bridge
text: Taken from the west bridge, the Weeping Water Creek near flood stage. Tom Sorensen, Sr. home top center. Photo by Fred Ward.

title: Looking south on Main Street
text: Looking south on Main Street, intersection flooded by drainage ditch.

title: The new footbridge
text: The new footbridge connecting the tennis courts and Weeping Water lakes had to be anchored by rope to a nearby tree. Water level raised even higher.

title: Water Over The Dam
text: Not much resemblance between the usually placid Weeping Water Creek and this stretch of angry water. This shot was taken Monday morning looking south when the high waters reached Weeping Water and came boiling over the dam just west of the City Park. Every once in awhile, Mother Nature just has to let you know whose boss.

title: River Stay Away From My Door
text: Mr. and Mrs. Tom Sorensen's home and yard at flood stage Monday morning. Excessive rainfall along the Weeping Water watershed raised waters to flood stage here. The Sorensens have had to leave their home more than once during past spring floods. So far this year, they have been lucky.—Fred Ward Photos.

title: Watershed History Has Been One Of Floods, Project Delays
text: 1939—the Cass-Otoe soil conservation district was formed with the water conservation district formed later. 1950—the Weeping Water community club was formed for the express purpose of addressing the flooding problems. In May and August of 1950 there were two floods. 1951—the Cass Weeping Water watershed district was formed. Also in that year there was another flood. 1954—more flooding recorded. 1964—the Weeping Water Creek watershed steering committee was formed, staying together for three years, until 1967. During this time period, committee members collected damage reports from landowners in the watershed area whose land was damaged by flooding. Also, in 1964 more flooding was recorded. 1966—as a result of the damage reports compiled by the watershed steering committee, an application for planning assistance was submitted to federal authorities, the Soil Conservation Service (SCS). 1969—the Weeping Water Creek watershed conservancy district was formed. ... June, 1970—the State Natural Resources committee granted a tentative planning priority. July, 1972—the natural resources districts (NRD) came into being, 24 of them, replacing 155 smaller districts having similar goals. 1972—both the SCS and the State soil and water conservation service office submitted plans for flood prevention within the watershed. 1973—the Weeping Water watershed area proponents found themselves listed 20th in priority. June, 1975—the list of the top 20 watershed districts across Nebraska were set for priority re-evaluation, at which time the Weeping Water watershed was moved up to sixth place overall. However only the top five projects were sent off for planning. 1978-79—the U.S. bureau of reclamation conducted a study of the Weeping Water watershed for Cass and Otoe counties and concluded that the project was not feasible for funding. March, 1979—12 years after the original application was sent off, in 1967, ... the Weeping Water watershed proposal along with three others [went] to the SCS for a new study. 1981—the SCS again returned a verdict that the Weeping Water watershed was not feasible for funding. June, July, 1982—flooding recorded.

title: NRD Promises Action During '80s In Weeping Water Watershed Area
text: Approximately 170 persons attended a meeting Thursday evening, Aug. 26, at the community building in Nehawka on the topic of flood prevention and land resources management along the Weeping Water creek watershed flood plain and watershed area. ... Bill Whipple of Union and DeForest Brown, Weeping Water, present at the meeting Thursday night, noted they were among a group of people who began efforts in 1950 trying to get floodwater protection for the Weeping Water watershed area and flood plain.

title: Flood Crest Goes to All-Time High
text: The worst flood in the history of Weeping Water swept down the valley Sunday afternoon, knocking out the municipal water plant for the third time this month, and adding to the damage of the two previous June inundations. Homes along the creek were flooded. The old power house at the west bridge, weakened in the overflow two weeks ago, was almost completely wrecked. A Keckler Oil Co. storage tank that was left on the creek bank at the west bridge in the June 4 flood, floated away, damaging both downtown bridges. J. I. Corley, Weeping Water resident for 65 years, said the Weeping Water Creek went to the highest level in his memory. ... The channel was left at least 10 feet wider in the middle of town ... Rain measuring 4.12 inches at the official station in Weeping Water sent the creek up rapidly shortly after noon, and the torrent was increased by water that came roaring down the creek from cloudbursts in the vicinity of Wabash, Elmwood and Eagle. ... Radio stations sent out alarming reports about the situation here, and dozens of persons came from all over Cass County to see the flood. A special bus brought a group from Louisville. The oil tank pounded at the west bridge as the water rose and fell during the afternoon, bending some of the steel framework. With one dramatic stroke, the current swept the tank under the bridge late in the day. The bridge heaved as the tank went under, the tank crashing at the framework underneath and ripping at the wooden sidewalk. Dozens of people, who had been watching at the bridge, waiting for this to take place, ran up the alley towards the east bridge, expecting to see the tank sweep the bridge away with it. ... The tank struck with a heavy thud, the bridge groaned and swayed. The crowd grew and watched until dark ... Water Situation Acute: ... There was only a small supply in the city reservoir when the flood struck, and by midnight all this had been drained away. Water was brought into town in tin cans Monday, and bottled drinks were selling fast.

title: Water reaches highest point in history
text: Upper photo—Crest of Sunday's flood as seen from the dam between the two lakes, looking towards waterworks (extreme right). Middle—Waterworks and Keckler bulk oil station, photographed from railroad culvert over north branch. Lower—James P. Howland prepares to lash an oil tank to the railroad tracks, after wading through water up to his hips to pull the tank away from the old power house, where it lodged after a flood earlier this month. Behind him is Frank Garrison, while Richard Keckler, in swim trunks, is shown in center background. (Photos by The Republican.)

title: Many Bridges Lost in Floods
text: Bond issue imperative to solve problem. A bond issue is probably the only solution to the dilemma in which Cass County finds itself in the matter of bridges as the result of disastrous June floods ... Swedetown Bridge County Loss: Also lost in the flood was the Swedetown bridge in Weeping Water, and some officials were of the opinion that the county was responsible ...

title: Creek Overflows Again Wednesday For Third Week
text: Cass County experienced floods on Weeping Water Creek yesterday for the third consecutive Wednesday. Lowlands in the vicinity of Union were under water, and Missouri Pacific tracks between Nehawka and Union were covered. Passenger trains did not run yesterday. Rain fell in Weeping Water Wednesday and Thursday morning, although the creek was well within its banks. ... Ralph Keckler, who suffered heavy loss two weeks ago when his gasoline storage tanks floated away ...

title: Water Supply Poses Problem
text: Is declared safe, but many are boiling it. Weeping Water people have found the city water supply murky for the past ten days, as the result of floods. ... Five times the normal amount of chlorine is going into the water.

title: Rebuilding after the floods of 1950
text: UPPER left shows "Gopher" Lauritzen coming out of the ground near the connection of the main on the south side in front of the home of Mr. and Mrs. L. E. Johnson. Our local water commissioner was unaware that we took his picture. UPPER right shows the Parker Construction Co. crew at work on the new main of the water system leading under the creek to the south part of Weeping Water. The old main developed several leaks during the May flood this year and required new pipe under the creek. The south side was supplied with water by a temporary main across the bridge. LOWER left shows the pileup of the Swedetown bridge, washed away in the 1947 flood and the east Weeping Water bridge washed away this year. A salvage crew of the Parker Construction Co. pulled steel girders and planking from the creek to supply materials for two footbridges to be constructed across the Weeping Water.

title: Flood Takes a Heavy Toll (Louisville, Mill Creek)
text: Twelve Lives Taken in Flood—Homes and Bridges Swept Away. Friday, September 28th, proved to be "Black Friday" in Louisville. About 5:30 the storm started with little wind, but the rain fell in such torrents that about 7 o'clock Mill Creek, that runs through the city, was out of its banks and for about three hours the town was swept by a flood. One of the merchants told a reporter that the first wave that came was five feet high. He said the first he knew of the flood he heard people calling in the streets—"Fly to the hills." ... Mr. and Mrs. George Schoeman, 88 and 76 years of age, who live alone, was one of the most thrilling rescues made. The water rushed down upon them six feet high and broke over their little home which stood on the bank of Mill Creek; the house was caught in the flood and swung toward the creek, but was caught by big trees which saved their lives.

title: Piloted Autos Thru Flood: Teamsters at Union Cleaned Up $500
text: It is estimated that teamsters at Union earned $500 piloting autos through the flood waters of the Weeping Water creek, crossed by the Federal highway at that place. Following is an account of this, taken from the Union Unison: The Weeping Water was bank full and overflowing, the water having even reached half-way up the road to Union. This made travel to and from the bridge dangerous and as there was very little rain either north or south of Union the travel was not discontinued and as a result there were many cars waiting to cross this angry stretch of water. Men with teams to the number of from four to six were kept busy until late at night plying their dangerous traffic of safely conducting timid drivers across this pond. Such men as Frank Anderson, Charlie Hathaway, Sherman Austin and a few others were encountering danger every trip when they agreed to make these trips over with a car for the price of a dollar a car. However, after dark the price was raised and there was not one traveler who thought the price unfair for the work. One man hauled as many as twenty-five teams and ...

title: Heavy Rain Storm Here Last Sunday
text: The citizens of Cass county began to fear that the long awaited and devastating flood waters would cover the low lands of this section last Sunday afternoon when the heavy rain with hail and wind hit this section with force about three o'clock in the afternoon. ... Weeping Water was very fortunate that the storm was no more heavy than it was. In other sections of the county, especially at Louisville, rains in the proportions of a cloud burst fell. Citizens in that section were reminded all too vividly of the terrible flood which hit there a few years ago, when several lives were lost. ... The Weeping Water creek was soon a roaring torrent of water, rising very rapidly, and for a time, it looked as though it would go out of its banks. However, the water began to recede before it had become bank full and no danger was evidenced.

title: Watching the swirling waters
text: Mr. and Mrs. Ray Knott and daughter, and 2 unidentified boys, stand in the yard of the home of Mr. and Mrs. Tom Sorensen and family and watch the swirling waters of the flooding Weeping Water creek last Saturday morning. As the photo shows, water came within inches of flooding the Sorensen home, which is located on East street, between the railroad tracks and the creek. A group of volunteers had helped Sorensen remove several appliances and other articles of furniture shortly before this picture was taken. The waters started receding shortly thereafter.—Photo by Fred Ward

title: Watershed Need Illustrated By Week End Storm
text: "As we all know, this area experienced extensive flood damage," said a local Watershed booster. "This flood followed less than a year the June 1964 flood in which the residents of the Weeping Water Creek Watershed then expressed a desire to form a watershed district to cope with such storms and prevent the waste and destruction which always follows. Let's take a lesson from the Lincoln area and get together and push our watershed to completion. Only then can we feel secure that our lives and property are well protected when such storms come."

title: Remains of swinging bridge
text: The tangled mess above is what remains of the swinging bridge over the Weeping Water creek. The bridge provided a walk-way for residents living in the Riverside Addition to cross the creek to East P Street. Unless or until this is replaced, children walking to school will have to go around via Garfield Street to Eldora and S. East Street. This will also necessitate crossing the Missouri Pacific railroad tracks twice.

title: Debris packed against railroad trestle
text: The picture above shows the June 15 flooding aftermath. Ordinarily, this railroad trestle spans a road running north and south approximately three miles east and one-half mile south of Weeping Water near the Vernon Duwe farm. Lifter and silt were also found on top of the track. The debris is packed solid around the bridge supports.

title: What is left of the west bridge
text: Tyrus S. Gilliam and Greg Swanson, Omaha, District Representatives for Congressman Hal Daub, were in Weeping Water Thursday morning surveying the flood damage. Mayor Wayne Rupp is showing, with Gilliam near, what is left of the west bridge now lying on the creek bank just below the Tom Sorensen home.—Photo by Fred Ward. Weeping Water was the first community out of 31 counties in Nebraska to seek help in making application for emergency funds.

title: Weeping Water Creek leaves banks Monday
text: Right now a guaranteed contract reading, "It ain't gonna rain no more, no more," would be signed by every individual in the Weeping Water area. The torrential rains which bombarded Nebraska Sun. and early Mon. once again raised the Weeping Water Creek to flood stage. Water poured over the banks of the creek, flooding the tennis courts, gardens along the creek banks, into the Bickford Track Field, threatening residents along River, S. Elm, East P and the Sorensen home on S. East Streets. ... Mrs. Tom Sorensen Sr. alerted the Fire Dept. at 5 a.m. Mon. concerning the rising waters. Later several assisted in moving Mr. and Mrs. Bruce Sorensen from the Sorensen home on East Street. The Bruce Sorensens had just moved into the home on Sun. They moved back in Tues. evening. Mrs. Tom Sorensen had stored canned vegetables and fruit in the basement there and worked removing them until water started coming down the basement stairs. The house ended up with about three feet of water in the basement but none came into the ground floor of the home. ... Having gone through a disastrous flood just one year ago, Weeping Water residents had no desire for a repeat.

title: Overflows
text: OVERFLOWS—The Weeping Water Creek which had remained within its banks during the spring and earlier this summer went over the top flooding the tennis courts and other lowland ground in the vicinity.

title: Not Much Flood Damage Here
text: Heavy rain ... caused the Weeping Water creek to rise to flood stage ... For a time Tuesday night, it was feared the creek would get into the Tom Sorensen home. A county bridge, located approximately 3 1/2 miles west of Weeping Water, was damaged during the storm ...

title: Around Town: a sizeable chunk of ice
text: ...fog... snow... ice... sleet... rain... blizzard... you name it, the great State of Nebraska has it all, especially the southeast corner... we forgot to mention flood along with the rain... a very sizeable chunk of ice was deposited on the north edge of Weeping Water on the edge of the Tom Sorensen, Sr., property... the creek was over its banks Friday nite... let's hope this welcome warm weather doesn't result in the flooding predicted along the Platte and other rivers...

title: The Flood of 1993 hits Weeping Water
text: After weeks of rainy weather and reports of flooding throughout the midwest, the inevitable happened early Friday morning, July 23. The Weeping Water Creek turned into a swift flowing river, flooding homes, businesses, and farm ground throughout the valley. Heavy rain began to fall late Thursday night and continued into the daylight hours on Friday morning. Approximately seven inches fell on the Weeping Water area with the heaviest recorded between midnight and 4 a.m. Flooding occurred all along the banks of the Weeping Water Creek. High water was reported at the west end of Weeping Water's main street where the Gospel Run Creek had backed up. Countryside Heating and Air Conditioning was flooded and there were around five feet of water in the basement of the fire hall. ... Some residents of Swedetown were evacuated while others, on higher ground, remained in their homes. ... According to Fire Chief Larry Hanson, about a dozen Weeping Water residents were evacuated. ... Although the sewage plant was completely surrounded by water, it was not damaged. The city shop and garage building was not so lucky. Water poured through the doors of the structure, ripping tin and twisting the building. ... The swinging bridge, connecting Weeping Water and Swedetown, sustained considerable damage. ... According to officials the Weeping Water Creek rose three feet within one hour. It crested at 23 feet at Weeping Water shortly after dawn. Flood stage at Weeping Water is between 11 and 12 feet depending upon where you are. ... Weeping Water has received 18.87 inches of rain in July through midnight Mon., July 26. This measurement is 15.12 above normal for the entire month of July. ... The last time Weeping Water experienced three days in a row without precipitation were enjoyed was April 21.

title: A 150-year-old oak finds a new home
text: THIS 150 YEAR old Nationally Registered Oak tree found a new home atop and in the farm home of Dale and Nancy Nutzman and family, south of the Beaver lake area. (Photo by Jean Thomassen)

title: West bridge looking north to Main Street
text: WEST BRIDGE LOOKING NORTH TO MAIN STREET—Swift water pounded relentlessly against the east bridge and surrounded it during the Friday flood, but it held fast. Due to the high water, it was closed from approximately 1:30 a.m. Friday morning until 6:30 p.m. Friday evening. (Photo by Jackie Salberg)

title: The remainder of the swinging bridge
text: THE REMAINDER OF THE SWINGING BRIDGE—Built in 1951, the swinging bridge spanning the Weeping Water Creek at the end of East P Street has undergone renovation twice due to high water. Friday's flood twisted both approaches, but left them attached to the main section of the bridge. The bridge connected Weeping Water and Swedetown and served as a short cut to school for the children on the east side of the creek. (Photo by Jackie Salberg)

title: The oak tree, aftermath
text: A GREAT DEAL of the huge 150 year old oak tree remains lodged against the Nutzman home, as workers and their chain saws removed sections of the tree and others hauled the limbs away. (Photo by Jean Thomassen)

title: Looking north from East P Street
text: LOOKING NORTH from the east end of East P Street. Flood water surrounded the City shop and garage and sewage treatment facility. This photo was taken around 10:30 a.m. on Friday morning after the creek had crested at 23 feet at Weeping Water and waters were beginning to recede. (Photo by Jackie Salberg)

title: River Street was a river
text: RIVER STREET WAS A RIVER—The east end of West River Street and the Weeping Water Creek were one about 9 a.m. on Friday morning, July 23. A portion of Antoniette Hohman's garage is pictured in the foreground. Her car was trapped inside. (Photo by Jackie Salberg)

title: Threatening waters
text: THREATENING WATERS—Bernie Moore's home on East P Street was among the many to be invaded by water from the rampaging Weeping Water Creek. Although the basement of this residence was flooded, the upstairs level sustained very little flood damage. (Photo by Jackie Salberg)

title: Flood Sweeps Eastern Nebraska; Tragedy of the Storm
text: A flood, which from reports, swept the greater part of eastern Nebraska ... caused a great deal of damage in Cass county last Thursday night and Friday morning. The estimated rainfall in Weeping Water was between six and seven inches, washing out bridges, railroad tracks, flooding cellars ... Several carloads of rip-rap have been shipped out of Weeping Water to repair damage done by the flood ... The creek at Weeping Water was out of its banks and running over the bottom land, flooding everything in its way. At the city pump house, water rose to such a depth that the motors were put out of commission, and the city was out of water until Tuesday noon ... From Union, the report came to us Friday morning around 11 o'clock that the water was at the water tower and still rising. ... Tragedy of the Storm: The greatest tragedy of the entire storm in this part of the community was at Nehawka, where Dr. Douglas E. Hansen was drowned in the swollen Weeping Water creek while making an attempt to reach the bedside of a patient. ... Dr. Hansen was called to the Nelson Berger home early Friday morning. Being unable to cross the swollen stream in his car, due to some four feet of water running over the fill south of Nehawka, Dr. Hansen borrowed a horse and attempted to ford the avalanche of water. From all appearance the horse became frightened and slipped from the grade, carrying its rider with it. Rescue parties patrolled the stream, which was reported as being a half mile wide, through the entire day, and about four o'clock the body was recovered about 100 feet from where it had gone into the water. Dr. Hansen is well known in this community, having practiced in this part of the county for about two years. He came to Weeping Water often to play golf and mix with the boys in a general way, always having a smile and a cheery word for those who knew him.

title: Firemen to Rescue
text: Last Sunday evening, when the fire whistle sounded out the warning that there was a fire in the city, citizens' hearts sank, because each one knew that the water supply had run out, due to the flood waters putting the motors at the pump house out of commission. When the report was given out that a gasoline pump at the Dowler garage was on fire, the thought of danger grew. ... Everyone expected to hear a loud report and see flames thrown over the surrounding buildings, causing a great deal of damage. Due to the presence of mind and cooperation of the firemen the blaze was soon quenched before it had gained a great deal of headway, due to the heavy supply of chemicals always held in readiness for such emergencies.

title: 40 Years Ago: fish with gas on their stomachs
text: 40 YEARS AGO: Weeping Water is digging out from the most devastating flood ever to hit the community. The swirling waters of the Weeping Water Creek and its tributaries paralyzed transportation, crippled the water system, closed the schools and damaged at least one dozen homes. For the first time in Weeping Water, milk was available in half-gallon cartons. Most of the fish caught east of town seem to be saturated with gasoline. Consequently their food value is considerably impaired. In other words, if you eat these fish, you will really have gas on your stomach.

title: Flood reminder: Bruce Sorensen digs out the tennis courts
text: FLOOD REMINDER—Some 10 inches of dirt is being removed from the tennis courts in Weeping Water by City Employee Bruce Sorensen. The mud was deposited on the courts when the Weeping Water Creek flooded May 26.

title: Bankfull
text: BANKFULL—Water in the Weeping Water Creek is ready to overflow in this photo. The stream flooded the tennis courts and got to the railroad tracks after the six inches of rain Tuesday. The west bridge was closed because of high water and a large log caught on the west side. Fire trucks barricaded the bridge so no one could walk or drive across. (Photo by Diane Puls).

title: Letter: Another flood on the Weeping Water Creek
text: Dear Editor, Another flood on the Weeping Water Creek. There is no other town on the Weeping Water Creek that is affected like Weeping Water. The tennis court is flooded, the dam in the creek that has fed water to the lakes is gone. The lakes will be just two mud holes. Of course everyone gets concerned when the creek floods, but after a few days, when it dries up, forget all about it. ... So, it can only be said, if you are at all interested in soil and water erosion and flood control, be there and express your ideas. Buzz Brown, Weeping Water

title: Creek alignment between bridges in Weeping Water gets NRD help
text: Directors of the Lower Platte South Natural Resources District agreed to spend up to $5,000 on a channel realignment project on the Weeping Water Creek between the two bridges in Weeping Water. The action took place at the Oct. 21 meeting held in Lincoln. ... The NRD will participate with the City of Weeping Water in reducing a curve in the creek and in rip-rapping along the banks. The project will be a 50-50 cost sharing arrangement.

title: Weeping Water project approved for funding by Commission
text: The long-studied project of flood control for the Weeping Water Creek Watershed has reached a historic milestone. In November, the project to construct twenty flood control dams received approval from the Nebraska Natural Resources Commission for state funding of 75% of the total cost of $5.2 million. ... The watershed drains 262 square miles in Cass and Otoe counties into Weeping Water Creek which runs from Alvo on the west through Elmwood, Weeping Water, Avoca, Nehawka and Union, and enters the Missouri River southeast of Union. The largest flood on record was in May 1950 with a peak flow of 60,000 cubic feet per second at Union. The second largest flood, and the most economically damaging flood, was in June 1984, estimated to have caused more than $6 million in damages. The most recent floods occurred in June 1987 and in September 1989. ... Before any of the twenty dams will be constructed, the Lower Platte South NRD has set a requirement that 80% of the lands draining into the dams must be protected from excessive soil erosion. ... The Weeping Water Creek Watershed Project is the largest project approved by the State for assistance from the Nebraska Resources Development Fund. In addition, it will be the first comprehensive watershed project of this magnitude to be constructed in Nebraska that is not under a Federal Program. While this project will not completely eliminate the flooding problem in the watershed, it will significantly reduce the damages ...

title: Summer construction moves flood control project to its halfway point
text: The earth will soon be moving in Cass County as five flood control dams have been given the go-ahead for construction. The dams are the next component in the Weeping Water Watershed Flood Control Project which involved the installation of 19 dams along Weeping Water Creek and its tributaries. Six dams were completed last year and a seventh structure is under contract for construction this summer. By the beginning of 1996, the project will be 50 percent complete. ... The permanent pool area of the dams will range from 4 to 17 acres. When the Weeping Water Project is complete, average annual flood damages will be reduced by nearly 38 percent in the watershed. More than 250 square miles will be protected from future floods. ... The entire project is scheduled to be finished in the year 2000.

title: Landmark repaired
text: LANDMARK REPAIRED—The swinging bridge spanning the Weeping Water Creek between Swedetown and Weeping Water is once again ready to be used. Flood waters in July of this year twisted both approaches and covered the bridge with debris. Dale Nielsen and crew, along with Hank Friesel, who served as chief engineer, repaired the bridge.

title: Waterball anyone?
text: WATERBALL ANYONE?—This photo of the basketball courts in Weeping Water was taken on Sunday morning. Heavy rains during the week and into the weekend caused the Weeping Water Creek to flow out of its banks. Weeping Water received over four inches of rain last week. The National Weather Service blames this "monsoon" like season on the lingering effects of El Niño. (Photo by Cathy Stander)

title: Swinging Bridge
text: The swinging foot bridge spanning the Weeping Water Creek, at the end of East P Street in Weeping Water, is as useful as it is unique. Built in 1951 to replace the traffic bridge which was washed out by the flood of 1950, it served as a shortcut for the children in Swedetown going to and from school. Henry Friesel, along with Albert Jacobsen and Rasmus Lauritzen, constructed the bridge using city funds. Henry, who lives in Swedetown, has more or less been keeper of the bridge since it was built. The bridge has undergone renovations twice since 1951.

title: Cass County watches the skies (May 1987)
text: Heavy thunderstorms Monday evening, May 25, and Tues., May 26, forced Mill Creek out of its banks and left several Louisville homeowners heading for Red Cross shelters. ... Further south, residents along the Weeping Water Creek loaded sandbags to prevent seepage into basements and watched. "The creek was at least six and one half feet above flood stage at 9 a.m. Tuesday," said Betty Harms of the Weeping Water Rescue team. "Flood stage on the creek is about nine feet," she said, adding that one rescue worker suffered a broken arm while sandbagging.

title: The creek threatens homes
text: ... the Weeping Water Creek threatened homes in Weeping Water Tuesday. Officials said the creek receded considerably Wednesday afternoon. (Photo by Fred Ward)

title: Two boys, one canoe, and a raging creek
text: Sorely needed rain fell on Weeping Water and most of the state Monday. Before the downpour finally stopped an official 4.96 inches of rain had fallen here. According to Archie Crozier, official U.S. Weather Observer, the total was greatest to fall in a 24-hour period since the flood of May 8, 1950. ... Two Weeping Water youths, Gary Wiles, son of Mr. and Mrs. Kenneth Wiles, and Joe Ward, son of Mr. and Mrs. Fred Ward, had a narrow escape Monday afternoon. The two boys embarked on a canoe trip down the creek, when the water was at its highest. They entered the creek near the Wiles farm, 3 1/2 miles west of Weeping Water. They encountered no great difficulty until they tried to go over the dam just west of the City Lakes. At this point the raging waters overturned the canoe, throwing the boys into the swirling water. Ward was able to grab a tree limb and managed to get out of the creek a short distance from the point where the canoe overturned. Wiles was not so fortunate. He was swept downstream, but was finally lucky enough to be able to climb on top of the overturned canoe. He rode the canoe about a mile downstream before a group of men finally pulled him from the creek at the footbridge just east of the Jim Doyle home. The men, Lloyd Lane, Jed Friesel, and Leon Wendt, lowered a rope to Wiles just as he started to pass under the bridge. He was able to get a loop over his shoulders and the men pulled him out. They said it was all they could do to hold him when the current caught him after he slipped off the canoe.

title: Nehawka: Sudden Thaw Raises Creek Highest Seen
text: Water from thawing snow running into the Weeping Water creek caused it to overflow Wednesday morning and before the water receded it reached the highest stage ever seen by the residents of Nehawka. ... Snow melted very fast and ice began to break up in the creek. An ice gorge formed a short distance east of the bridge and about ten o'clock the water in the creek backed up and the road between the tracks and the bridge was flooded. The ice gorge went out about the noon hour and the creek continued to raise flooding all low lands along the course of the stream. ... The water ran over the old wagon bridge south of town and the heavy ice did considerable damage to the bannisters on the structure. ... The low land belonging to V. P. Sheldon southeast of town was also flooded. The water here was a regular lake, backing up from the creek and water reaching the lower seat in the grand stand at the ball park. ... School children from the country who reached school in the morning were kept in town by various families for the night. The high water attracted almost everyone in town to the creek bank at some time during the day and it was a real curiosity to everyone who saw it. ... V. P. Sheldon's large red barn south of the Sheldon factory was on an island.

title: Big Rains Visit This Section and Helps Make Big Potato Crop
text: The anticipated drougth was prevented by heavy rains which came on Monday night, Tuesday and Tuesday night to the grand total of over 5 inches. Up to Tuesday evening the precipitation was 3.31 inches, then during the night another deluge of 1.75 inches came. The creek went out of its banks and damaged fields and gardens, it being the highest it has been for a long time. ... Rain was needed for the potato crop which is insured now.

title: 4.19 Inches of Rain Fell Here Saturday Afternoon
text: Rainfall of cloudburst proportions hit Weeping Water and surrounding area Saturday afternoon. The rain was accompanied by two very heavy hail storms. Total rainfall for Weeping Water was 4.19 inches ... The little drainage creek, which runs from the north part of town, past the Christian church and into the Weeping Water creek east of the lake, was too big for its bridges. It stayed out of its banks for almost two hours. Water and mud once again found their way into the home of Mrs. John McGrady, but not to the extent of the 1950 flood. A garage belonging to Ed Lorensen was almost filled with a collection of cornstalks, brush and other debris. A number of lawns were covered with several inches of mud, gravel, crushed rock, etc. ... The flood water reached the very top of cement guards around the basement windows of the Don Rutledge home, but did not get into the basement. Four years ago, when the home belonged to C. E. Nutter, heavy damage resulted ...

title: Heavy Rainfall Last Saturday Proves Conservation's Worth
text: The heavy downpour in the Manley, Weeping Water, Avoca area on May 15 showed that it still can rain hard in Nebraska, and that when it does, proper conservation measures well maintained do a good job of controlling erosion, reports Earl Cook, of the local SCS unit. ... Bare fields suffered most from the rain, SCS men stated. Earl Puls, 2 miles northwest of Manley, reported 2 1/2 in. of rain in 1 1/2 hours and flood water as high as in the 1950 flood. He is glad he had part of his farm protected by terraces. ... Chris Stohlmann, 2 miles north of Manley, says 2 inches of rain fell in 45 minutes. His terraces did a good job. ... Rains such as this emphasize the need for complete conservation treatment of all land to control erosion, according to SCS workers. Large amounts of plant cover on top of the soil, terraces with good channel capacity maintained, and good grass waterways are among the most important erosion control measures.

title: Cass-Weeping Water Watershed Organized Last Thursday
text: Stan Matzke, farm editor of the Lincoln Journal, was the main speaker at the organizational meeting of the Cass-Weeping Water Creek Watersheds association, held last Thursday night in the auditorium at Weeping Water. Mr. Matzke explained at length his views on soil conservation and its part in flood control. His talk was educational and informative and was well received by the crowd of over 150 farmers, businessmen, housewives and children present. ... The purpose of the watershed association is to hold the water on the land where it falls. This is accomplished with soil conservation practices—terraces, contour farming, grassed waterways, etc. After this work is done, small flood storage dams will be built at the lowest point of the watershed. Larger storage dams will be built downstream to hold back the water from the heavier rainstorms. ... There are already 1,600 miles of terraces built in the Cass-Weeping Water watershed. WATERSHED OFFICERS—Newly elected officers of the Cass-Weeping Water Creek Watershed association at Weeping Water preside over the board of directors meeting. They are (from left) Co-chairman Art Wolph, Nehawka; Elmer Stoehrs, Cedar Creek, vice-chairman; Paul Fauquet, Plattsmouth, acting secretary; Joe Bender, Weeping Water co-chairman.—Lincoln Journal Photo.

title: Watershed project gets more work from NRD
text: By approving "in concept" the first stage of a planning process that could eventually control flooding along Weeping Water Creek in Cass County, the Lower Platte South Natural Resources District (NRD) last week authorized the negotiations with an Omaha engineering firm for a more detailed feasibility study of that plan. The planning concept approved by the NRD board calls for an estimated $10.1 million worth of structural measures which are designed to reduce by 60 percent the future floods along Weeping Water Creek and its tributaries in the 160,000-acre drainage area. Based on a goal of a 60 percent reduction in flood damages, and the desire of local residents for a solution to their flooding and erosion problems which emphasizes small farm impoundments, the preliminary plan for the watershed calls for one large reservoir on the creek, northwest of Elmwood, seven small structures on the Creek's tributaries and 186 farm ponds. ... "The concept we're working with at the present time offers a 40 cent return for each dollar spent on the project over its 50 year life," Johnson said.

title: NRD board member from Cass defends watershed sinking fund
text: As part of the new budget, $200,000 is to be placed in a sinking fund slated for future dam construction in the Weeping Water watershed, running almost the entire length of Cass County, from Alvo to the Missouri River. While some NRD board members criticized the $200,000 sinking fund, Ron Bertsch, a board member from Plattsmouth, stuck up for the Watershed proposal. Board member Keith Myers, Lincoln, stated his objection to the sinking fund, stating that it is projected the 58 dams will return only 50 cents for every dollar spent on conservation measures. ... "Weeping Water did not increase the levy, Deadman's Run increased the levy," concluded Bertsch.

title: 12,307 acre feet storage provided by watershed plan
text: The Directors of the Lower Platte South NRD selected a $7.9 million flood control plan for the Weeping Water Creek Watershed which calls for the construction of 58 reservoirs and achieves a 55.6% annual average flood damage reduction. In choosing what was called "Plan A" the directors opted for a plan that will provide 12,307 acre feet of flood water storage throughout the 261 square mile drainage area and which will require 57 "dry" field reservoirs ranging in size from 5.8 acres to 63.5 acres. This plan also calls for the construction of one major reservoir located about one mile northwest of Nehawka which in addition to flood control will also provide recreational benefits.
